A piece of cake
a piis ov kéik
Something very easy — Pan comido / está chupado.
The exam was a piece of cake.
Nothing to do with cake. Also: as easy as pie.
Break the ice
bréik di áis
Say or do something to start people talking — Romper el hielo.
He told a joke to break the ice.
Forms: breaks, broke, broken the ice. Noun: an icebreaker.
Spill the beans
spil da bíins
Reveal a secret — Irse de la lengua / descubrir el pastel.
Don't spill the beans about the party.
Forms: spills, spilled, spilled the beans. Same idea: let the cat out of the bag.
Let the cat out of the bag
let da kat áut ov da bag
Reveal a secret, often by accident — Descubrir el pastel / irse de la lengua.
She let the cat out of the bag at dinner.
Forms: lets, let, let the cat out of the bag.
Hit the sack
jit da sak
Go to bed — Irse al sobre / echarse a dormir.
I'm exhausted — I'm going to hit the sack.
Informal. Also: hit the hay. Forms: hits, hit, hit the sack.
Kill two birds with one stone
kil tuu berds uith uán stóun
Solve two problems with one action — Matar dos pájaros de un tiro.
I cycle to work and kill two birds with one stone.
Almost word for word the Spanish, which makes it easy to remember.
Cost an arm and a leg
kost an arm and a leg
Be extremely expensive — Costar un ojo de la cara / un riñón.
That watch cost an arm and a leg.
Forms: costs, cost, cost an arm and a leg.
Give someone the cold shoulder
guiv sámuan da kóuld shóulder
Deliberately ignore someone — Hacer el vacío a / dar de lado.
She gave me the cold shoulder all evening.
Also as a noun: get the cold shoulder.
Play it by ear
pléi it bai íir
Decide as you go instead of planning — Improvisar / sobre la marcha.
We have no plan — let's play it by ear.
From music: playing without written notes.
A pain in the neck
a péin in da nek
Someone or something very annoying — Un incordio / un pesado.
Filling in these forms is a pain in the neck.
Mildly rude versions exist; this one is safe.
Under the weather
ánder da uéder
Slightly ill — Pachucho/a / malito/a.
I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.
Gentle and very common; good for excusing yourself.
Hit the nail on the head
jit da néil on da jed
Say exactly the right thing — Dar en el clavo.
You've hit the nail on the head.
Forms: hits, hit, hit the nail on the head.
Up in the air
ap in di éer
Not decided yet — En el aire / sin decidir.
Our holiday plans are still up in the air.
Used with be: it is up in the air.
On the ball
on da bol
Quick to understand and react — Espabilado/a / al tanto.
The new assistant is really on the ball.
Used with be. Opposite: asleep at the wheel.
See eye to eye
sii ái tu ái
Agree completely with someone — Estar de acuerdo / verlo igual.
We don't see eye to eye on politics.
Usually in the negative. Pattern: see eye to eye with someone on something.
Over the moon
óuver da muun
Extremely happy — Encantado/a de la vida / loco/a de contento.
She was over the moon about the job.
Used with be. Mostly British English.
Speak of the devil
spiik ov da dévil
Said when the person you were discussing appears — Hablando del rey de Roma.
Speak of the devil — here he is!
The Spanish version is almost the same idea.
The spitting image
da spíting ímich
Exactly like someone in appearance — El vivo retrato / clavado/a.
He's the spitting image of his father.
Pattern: the spitting image of someone.
A rule of thumb
a ruul ov tham
A rough practical guide — Regla general / regla empírica.
As a rule of thumb, allow an hour per chapter.
The b in thumb is silent.
Over the top
óuver da top
Far too extreme — Pasado/a de rosca / exagerado/a.
The decorations were a bit over the top.
Often shortened to OTT in British English.
Keep an eye on
kiip an ái on
Watch something carefully — Vigilar / echar un ojo a.
Keep an eye on the soup while I answer the door.
Forms: keeps, kept, kept an eye on.
Actions speak louder than words
ákshans spiik láuder dan uérds
What you do matters more than what you say — Obras son amores y no buenas razones / hechos, no palabras.
He promised again, but actions speak louder than words.
A proverb; used whole, never changed.
Practice makes perfect
práktis méiks pérfect
You improve by doing something repeatedly — La práctica hace al maestro.
Keep going — practice makes perfect.
A proverb; used whole.
It is a small world
it is a smol uérld
Said when you meet someone unexpectedly — ¡Qué pequeño es el mundo!
You know my cousin? It's a small world.
Nearly always said as it's a small world.
Pie in the sky
pái in da skái
A hope that will never come true — Castillos en el aire / una quimera.
Free housing for everyone is pie in the sky.
Often used dismissively.
A race against time
a réis aguénst táim
A rush to finish before it is too late — Una carrera contrarreloj.
It was a race against time to save the crew.
Also: a race against the clock.
Caught red-handed
kot red-jánded
Caught in the act of doing wrong — Pillado/a con las manos en la masa.
The thief was caught red-handed.
Usually passive: be caught red-handed.
Throw in the towel
thróu in da táuel
Give up — Tirar la toalla.
After three failures he threw in the towel.
From boxing. Forms: throws, threw, thrown in the towel.
Shoot the breeze
shuut da bríiz
Chat casually about nothing important — Charlar / darle a la lengua.
We sat on the porch shooting the breeze.
Informal, American English. Forms: shoots, shot, shot the breeze.
Have something up your sleeve
jav sámthing ap yor sliiv
Have a secret plan ready — Tener un as en la manga.
He always has something up his sleeve.
Also: have an ace up your sleeve.
Get cold feet
guet kóuld fiit
Suddenly become too nervous to do something — Echarse atrás / entrarle miedo a uno.
He got cold feet the day before the wedding.
Forms: gets, got, got cold feet.
Once in a blue moon
uáns in a bluu muun
Very rarely — De higos a brevas / muy de vez en cuando.
We see each other once in a blue moon.
Goes at the end of the sentence or the start.
The last straw
da last stro
The final small thing that makes you lose patience — La gota que colma el vaso.
Losing my keys was the last straw.
From: the straw that broke the camel's back.
Bite the bullet
báit da búlit
Accept something unpleasant and get on with it — Apretar los dientes / hacer de tripas corazón.
I bit the bullet and went to the dentist.
Forms: bites, bit, bitten the bullet.
Beat around the bush
biit aráund da bush
Avoid saying the thing directly — Andarse por las ramas / dar rodeos.
Stop beating around the bush and tell me.
British English: beat about the bush. Forms: beats, beat, beaten.
Call it a day
kol it a déi
Stop working for now — Dejarlo por hoy.
It's late — let's call it a day.
Forms: calls, called, called it a day.
Cut to the chase
kat tu da chéis
Get to the important part at once — Ir al grano.
Cut to the chase — how much will it cost?
From film editing. Forms: cuts, cut, cut to the chase.
A blessing in disguise
a blésing in disgáis
Something bad that turns out well — No hay mal que por bien no venga.
Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
The s in disguise sounds like z.
Better late than never
béter léit dan néver
It is better to arrive or act late than not at all — Más vale tarde que nunca.
He apologised a year later — better late than never.
A proverb; used whole.
The ball is in your court
da bol is in yor kort
It is your turn to act or decide — La pelota está en tu tejado.
I've made my offer; the ball is in your court.
From tennis.
Miss the boat
mis da bóut
Be too late for an opportunity — Perder el tren / quedarse fuera.
If you don't apply now you'll miss the boat.
Forms: misses, missed, missed the boat.
On cloud nine
on kláud náin
Extremely happy — En una nube / en el séptimo cielo.
She's been on cloud nine since the news.
Used with be.
Out of the blue
áut ov da bluu
Completely unexpectedly — De repente / a bote pronto.
He called me out of the blue after ten years.
Goes at the end of the sentence.
Pull someone's leg
pul sámuans leg
Tease someone with something untrue — Tomar el pelo a.
Relax, I'm only pulling your leg.
Forms: pulls, pulled, pulled someone's leg.
